source.title: Decomposing the Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Joshua Engels; L. Smith; Max Tegmark

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE-based analysis to activations from Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1 language models and reports results bearing on SAE feature recovery and its limitations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SAE reconstruction error, its linear predictability, and downstream effects. It also discusses multidimensional representations in related work, but those cited findings are not results of this study. Values visible only in figures are not treated as numerical results unless the text describes them.
record.test_reason: On Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1 activations, the study measures how much Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs leave unexplained. It finds a nonlinear error floor that stays roughly constant as width scales, which bears on whether SAE features are a complete account (V5). It also runs a norm-prediction test on raw activations that bears on V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors find SAE error substantially predictable: about half the error vector, and over 90% of its norm. They split it into linear and nonlinear components and argue the nonlinear part is not unlearned linear features. Because it stays constant at fixed sparsity as SAEs scale, they argue for better SAEs rather than just bigger ones. Gradient pursuit reduces nonlinear error only very slightly; earlier-layer SAE outputs reduce it more.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses pretrained-language-model activations and SAE error analyses rather than toy networks with controlled sparse features, feature importance, and geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Error predictability varies with SAE width, L0, and layer; nonlinear FVU is approximately constant across width at fixed L0 in the examined middle layers, while other examined layers show some decrease that the authors say is uncertain.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-token SAE error norms of larger SAEs are highly predictable from those of smaller SAEs (Fig. 4, Fig. 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE scaling failures concentrate on the same contexts across dictionary sizes.

record.problems: No direct measurement of superposition geometry, neuron polysemanticity, or feature stability/canonicity. Several findings are based on plotted results without exact values in the text. Some decompositions rely on modeling assumptions; the authors note that linear error estimates may overestimate dense components and that synthetic random-vector tests did not behave as expected.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, phase transition or feature geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition measured.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity tested.
Spread of features across neurons is not measured. No direct count of recovered sparse features.
Stability and canonicality of features across seeds, dictionaries or methods are not tested. Only completeness is tested.
No direct search for or test of multi-dimensional features. The evidence is only an indirect norm-prediction test.

missing.what: Norm-prediction test R² for x, Sae(x), SaeError, LinearError and NonlinearError. The norm of x is near-perfectly predicted; the nonlinear error's norm is notably lower.
FVU_nonlinear roughly constant across SAE width at fixed L0 in middle layers, decreasing slightly at other layers. Power-law fit FVU 0.186+2.708W^-0.317 versus 0.122 with error prediction.
missing.locator: Section 4.3, Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Appendix A.2, Fig. 12

missing.what: Auto-interpretability: SAE latents trained on nonlinear error are about 5% less interpretable than those trained on linear error.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows concern the study's error-analysis tools rather than the claim itself, so they are unlinked or linked only to V5's completeness part. The V4 and V6 verdicts rest on text results that no row captures (Fig. 6) and are indirect. The authors note that the linear error estimate may overestimate the dense component, and that synthetic random-vector checks did not behave as expected.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or regular feature geometry are tested.
No neuron polysemanticity or competition for dedicated dimensions is measured.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons is tested.
The study analyzes SAE reconstructions and errors, not feature spread across neurons or a direct census of sparse features recovered.
The study investigates SAE reconstruction completeness, but not whether SAE features are stable or canonical across training runs, dictionaries, or methods.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature representations with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 2 9B, and Llama 3.1 8B (SAE results aggregated across combinations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a linear probe from model activations to squared SAE reconstruction-error norm.

conditions.value: Gemma Scope and Llama Scope; combinations of width, L0, layer, and model
about 247k activations from 300 Pile contexts; 150k training and 97k test activations

rows.measure: Test-set R² predicting squared SAE error norm
rows.value: 70%–95% of the variance explained across all combinations
rows.note: Error-norm predictability is reported, but it does not directly measure how many sparse features the SAE recovers.
rows.check: Predictability of the error norm is not itself a measure of sparse-feature recovery, spread or completeness. The study's reading of it as not-yet-learned features rests on its Appendix B model.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 2 9B, and Llama 3.1 8B (SAE results aggregated across combinations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a linear transformation from model activations to the SAE reconstruction-error vector.

conditions.value: Gemma Scope and Llama Scope; multiple widths, L0 values, and layers

rows.note: The result establishes predictable error components, not the identity or canonicality of the features represented by the SAEs.
rows.check: The authors read the 15–72% linearly predictable error as large linear subspaces SAEs fail to learn. This makes SAE coverage incomplete. The V4 link is dropped.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4 and 4.2; Figure 2 and Appendix A: error-vector prediction R² ranges from 15% to 72%.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Decompose error from a width 16k, L0 approximately 60 SAE into linearly predictable and nonlinear components; train new SAEs on each component.
rows.measure: Fraction of variance unexplained by new component-trained SAE
rows.value: nonlinear-error-trained SAE: approximately 0.59, an absolute 5 percentage points higher
rows.note: The nonlinear residual is harder for an SAE to reconstruct, supporting a limitation on SAE completeness; this does not establish whether learned features are canonical.
rows.check: Bears on completeness only. It shows a residual that is harder to learn (FVU ≈0.59 vs ≈0.54). V4 link dropped.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2: component-trained SAEs converge after about 100M tokens to FVU approximately 0.59 for nonlinear error and 0.54 for linear error.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Replace the layer activation with the SAE reconstruction plus one of the two error components and measure downstream cross-entropy loss recovery.

conditions.value: all tested layer 20 SAEs with L0 approximately 60 or width 16k

rows.measure: Percent of cross-entropy loss recovered relative to inserting only the SAE reconstruction and the normal model forward pass
rows.baseline: SAE reconstruction alone and normal model forward pass
rows.value: Both components contribute for the most part proportionally to their size; linear error may contribute slightly more than expected
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative comparison in text; detailed values are plotted. Residual error has downstream effects, but this is not a direct test of feature stability or canonicality.
rows.check: Shows both error components matter downstream roughly in proportion to size. Values are only plotted, so the size of the effect on completeness can't be read. V4 link dropped.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Apply gradient-pursuit inference-time optimization to frozen SAE decoder dictionaries, keeping the original reconstruction's L0.

conditions.value: Gemma Scope SAEs closest to L0 approximately 60

rows.measure: Total fraction of variance unexplained and nonlinear fraction of variance unexplained
rows.value: Total FVU decreases by 3%–5%; nonlinear FVU stays almost constant
rows.note: A more powerful encoder improves total reconstruction only modestly and leaves the nonlinear residual nearly unchanged.
rows.check: A better encoder cuts total FVU by 3–5%, but nonlinear FVU stays almost constant. The residual persists, so SAE reconstruction remains incomplete. V4 link dropped.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1 and Figure 9a: gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3–5%, with nonlinear FVU almost unchanged.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Regress SAE error components on SAE outputs for preceding residual-stream components.

conditions.value: width 16k, L0 approximately 60; layer 19 attention and MLP components
prior residual, attention, and MLP SAE outputs

rows.measure: R² of predicting SAE error components
rows.value: Prior components explain up to approximately 10% of total SAE error and between 4% and 14% of nonlinear error; the residual SAE output explains 50% of nonlinear-error variance
rows.note: The authors caution that the 50% result may be misleading because nonlinear error is partly a function of the SAE output. Results show substantial unexplained error remains.
rows.check: This is the study's method for reducing error (predicting it from prior-component SAE outputs), not a measure of the claimed behaviour.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Fit a scalar predictor from smaller-SAE per-token error norms to larger-SAE per-token error norms.
rows.measure: R² predicting larger-SAE per-token error norms
rows.value: Described as highly predictable overall; accuracy decreases as the SAEs get farther apart in scale
rows.note: No exact R² values are stated in the text. This measures shared error contexts, not sparse-feature recovery directly.
rows.check: Shows that small and large SAEs fail on the same tokens. This is a scaling-predictability result, not a test of a version. No R² value is stated in the text.

relationships.condition: Gemma Scope SAEs, Gemma 2 9B layer 20 (and Gemma 2 2B layer 12), fixed L0 ≈60, widths 16k–1M
relationships.reason: SAEs leave a residual. Part of it is linearly predictable unlearned subspace (r2). A nonlinear part is harder to learn (r3), is barely reduced by inference-time optimization (r5), and per the text stays roughly constant as width scales. So SAE dictionaries are incomplete and scaling may not close the gap.
relationships.display_finding: SAEs left a residual with a linearly predictable unlearned subspace and a nonlinear part that was harder to learn, barely reduced by inference-time optimization, and roughly constant as width scaled.

relationships.reason: Based on the text (no row): the squared norm of x is almost perfectly linearly predictable from x. The authors read this as x being well modeled as a sum of many 1-D features. The support is indirect.

relation.reason: The study measures unexplained activation content and tests whether dictionary scaling or improved inference removes it.

tranche.reason: Persistent reconstruction error and limited improvement from scaling or gradient pursuit qualify V5 completeness.

source_check.notes: The constant nonlinear-error floor is observed in the specified middle layers; Appendix A.2 reports some decrease with width elsewhere. Extrapolation to larger dictionaries is a hypothesis.

statements.correction: Section 4.2: error-vector prediction R² = 15%–72%. Sections 5.2 and 6.1: persistent reconstruction limitations. V5 verdict: limits_scope for the tested dictionaries.
statements.problem: The study's numerical result and incomplete-coverage interpretation are correct, but the challenges label overstates evidence of incomplete SAE coverage.

statements.correction: Section 5.1 and Figure 6: nonlinear-error squared norms are less linearly predictable; authors infer that this error is not a sparse sum of linear features from x. Appendix B.2: nonlinear error may largely reflect SAE-introduced approximation error. Superposed feature dimensionality is not determined.
statements.problem: The description of Section 5.1 is accurate, but reconstruction-error structure does not establish the dimensionality of superposed model features, so it does not justify a V6 limits_scope verdict.
